0.0.n: Adds emphasis to the speaker’s feeling.

0.1.n: Places the remembering in the present.

0.2.n: 思い出す in て-form plus よかった expresses happiness that something happened.

0.3.n: Adds a reflective, emotional tone to the thought before と.

0.4.n: Marks the preceding words as the thought expressed by 思う.

0.5.n: Plain present form introducing the speaker’s personal reflection.

0.6.n: Turns the preceding thought into a noun-like phrase: what the speaker thinks.

0.7.n: Marks that phrase as the topic, setting up what follows.

1.0.n: Names the destination of the journey.

1.1.n: Marks 学校 as the destination of 登校する.

1.2.n: 登校 plus する describes traveling to school, rather than studying there.

1.3.n: Follows 登校する to specify the occasion.

1.4.n: Marks the time described by 登校する時.

1.5.n: 自転車 names the bicycle; 乗り is the form of 乗る used before ながら, with に omitted casually.

1.6.n: Attaches to 乗り to show cycling happened at the same time as looking.

1.7.n: An everyday word for fields where rice is grown.

1.8.n: Marks 田んぼ as what the speaker was looking at.

1.9.n: Casual shortening of 眺めていた, describing an ongoing activity in the past.

1.10.n: Points to a particular scene in the speaker’s memory.

1.11.n: Names the remembered view described by the preceding phrase.

1.12.n: Marks the remembered scenery as what feels nostalgic in the next line.

2.0.n: Emphasizes the sincerity or strength of the feeling.

2.1.n: Contrasts the present viewpoint with the earlier school days.

2.2.n: Marks 今 as the point reached with なる, forming the idea of now that time has passed.

2.3.n: なる in たら-form usually means if or when; here 今になったら frames the speaker’s present perspective.

2.4.n: An emphatic spoken version of すごい, used casually here to strengthen an adjective.

2.5.n: 懐かしい expresses fond longing for the past; です makes the statement polite.

2.6.n: Links this feeling to another thought, suggesting it is part of a broader explanation.

3.0.n: Shows the speaker wants to repeat a previous experience.

3.1.n: A place name in Japan, used here as the destination.

3.2.n: Marks 岡山 as the destination of returning.

3.3.n: て-form of 戻る links returning to the following experience of nature.

3.4.n: Refers to the natural surroundings the speaker wants to experience.

3.5.n: Marks 自然 as what the speaker wants to feel.

3.6.n: 感じる changes to 感じたい to express the speaker’s desire.

3.7.n: Adds a wistful, personal tone to the wish before と.

3.8.n: Marks the wish as the content of 思います.

3.9.n: Describes the strength of the speaker’s thought or desire.

3.10.n: Polite present form of 思う, presenting the preceding wish as the speaker’s own thought.

3.11.n: Softens the ending and invites the listener to share the feeling.

0.lit: What I think, really, is I’m glad I remembered now, is—
0.tip: A verb in て-form followed by よかった means the speaker is glad that action happened.

1.lit: That scenery I was gazing at—rice fields while riding a bicycle when going to school—
1.tip: 乗りながら means while riding: ながら links two actions performed by the same person.

2.lit: Really, now that it’s now, it feels incredibly nostalgic, and—
2.tip: 今になったら emphasizes how things feel now, with the passage of time.

3.lit: Again, to Okayama return and nature want to feel, I strongly think, you know.
3.tip: A wish ending in たいな can be followed by と思います to express a reflective personal desire.
